# Dart Examples — sewpat

This folder demonstrates every dart feature provided by the `sewpat` library.
Each example uses the same simple **bodice-front block** (120 × 180 mm,
with a construction grid showing shoulder, bust, waist and hem lines) so the
geometry stays easy to follow across all five showcases.

Run all examples from the repo root to regenerate the SVGs:

```bash
python examples/darts/dart_examples.py
```

---

## What is a Dart? (Abnäher)

A dart is a stitched wedge that adds three-dimensional shaping to a flat
piece of fabric — the most common examples are bust darts and waist darts.

In `sewpat` a dart is always defined by **four points**:

| Point | Role |
|-------|------|
| `leg_a` / `leg_b` | The two mouth endpoints on the seam line |
| `center` | Mid-point of the mouth; the fold/crease line starts here |
| `tip` | The apex — where the dart is stitched to a point |

Secondary geometry (`width`, `depth`, `intake_angle`, stitching lines,
fold line) is derived automatically as properties.

---

## API Quick Reference

### Constructing a dart

**Direct construction** — supply all four points yourself:

```python
from sewpat import Dart, Point

dart = Dart(
    leg_a=Point(40, 100),
    leg_b=Point(60, 100),
    center=Point(50, 100),   # mouth midpoint
    tip=Point(50, 40),       # 60 mm deep
    fold_direction="inward", # "inward" (seam edge) or "outward" (inner panel)
    name="Taillennaht",
)
```

**`Dart.from_edge()` — place a dart directly on an existing seam edge:**

```python
from sewpat import Dart, Segment, Point, MM

waist_seam = Segment(Point(0, 110), Point(120, 110))

# Option A — explicit depth
dart = Dart.from_edge(
    waist_seam,
    position_t=0.55,    # 0 = start of edge, 1 = end
    width=22 * MM,
    depth=60 * MM,
)

# Option B — directed at a reference point (e.g. bust point)
dart = Dart.from_edge(
    waist_seam,
    position_t=0.55,
    width=22 * MM,
    reference_point=Point(75, 65),  # bust point
    tip_shortfall=25 * MM,          # stop 25 mm short of the bust point
)
```

Works equally well on a `CubicBezier` curved edge.

### Adding a dart to a PatternPart

```python
result = part.add_dart(
    dart,
    outer=True,          # True = seam-edge dart; False = inner rhombus dart
    notches=True,        # notch triangles at leg_a, leg_b (and mouth center)
    precision_tip=True,  # concentric circles at the tip
)
# result.stitch_elements, .fold_element, .cut_elements, .tip_elements, …
```

> **Order matters:** call `add_dart()` **before** `add_seam_allowance()`.
> The two cut-line segments are added to the outline with
> `seam_allowance=0.0` and `corner_join="miter"` so the SA engine folds
> cleanly across the dart mouth.

### Splitting a dart

```python
dart_a, dart_b = dart.split(ratio=0.5)  # equal halves; ratio ∈ (0, 1)
```

Both sub-darts share the same tip; the intake angle is divided
proportionally.

### Transferring a dart (pivot method)

```python
from sewpat import transfer_dart

transferred = transfer_dart(
    dart,
    new_edge=shoulder_seam,
    new_position_t=0.55,
)
```

The tip acts as the pivot. The intake angle and leg-to-tip distances are
preserved exactly; only the mouth is repositioned on the new edge.

---

## Example 1 — Outer Dart, Explicit Depth

A side-seam waist dart placed with `Dart.from_edge()` using a direct
depth value of 90 mm. This is the most basic use case.

**Rendered elements** (outer dart):
- Two dashed **stitching lines** (`leg_a → tip`, `leg_b → tip`)  
- One long-dash–dot **fold/crease line** (`center → tip`)  
- Two **cut-line outline segments** replacing the mouth region on the seam
  (with `seam_allowance=0.0` so the SA engine skips the wedge)  
- Small **notch triangle** at the mouth center (fold point after cutting)  
- **Notch triangles** at `leg_a` and `leg_b` perpendicular to the mouth edge  
- Two concentric **precision circles** at the tip with the dart name beside them

```python
side_seam = Segment(pts["shoulder_side"], pts["hem_side"])

dart = Dart.from_edge(
    side_seam,
    position_t=0.35,
    width=22 * MM,
    depth=90 * MM,
    fold_direction="inward",
    name="Taillennaht",
)
result = part.add_dart(dart, outer=True, notches=True, precision_tip=True)
```

![Example 1 – Outer dart, explicit depth](data:image/svg+xml;base64,))

## Example 2 — Outer Dart, Reference Point (Bust Point)

A side-seam **bust dart** aimed at the bust point. `tip_shortfall=25 mm`
keeps the tip 2.5 cm away from the bust point for ease and comfort.
The bust point itself is marked as a precision point.

```python
dart = Dart.from_edge(
    side_seam,
    position_t=0.38,             # at bust-line height on the side seam
    width=28 * MM,
    reference_point=pts["bust_point"],
    tip_shortfall=25 * MM,
    fold_direction="inward",
    name="Bustnaht",
)
```

![Example 2 – Bust dart aimed at the bust point](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

---

## Example 3 — Inner / Reverse Dart (Rhombus)

An inner dart on the bust line is rendered as a **rhombus (Raute)**:
four dashed stitching segments form a closed diamond shape
(`leg_a → tip → leg_b → center → leg_a`). Use this for princess-seam
style construction or any dart that opens inward.

```python
bust_line = Segment(pts["bust_cf"], pts["bust_side"])

dart = Dart.from_edge(
    bust_line,
    position_t=0.5,
    width=24 * MM,
    depth=55 * MM,
    fold_direction="outward",
    name="Eingriff",
)
result = part.add_dart(dart, outer=False, notches=True, precision_tip=True)
#                            ^^^^^^^^^^ rhombus mode
```

![Example 3 – Inner/reverse dart as rhombus](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Example 4 — Splitting a Dart

One large dart (36 mm wide) is split into two equal sub-darts (each
18 mm) with `Dart.split(ratio=0.5)`. The original dart is drawn in light
grey as a reference.  
Splitting is useful when a dart is too bulky to fold neatly, or when you
want to distribute the intake across two positions for a better fit.

```python
original = Dart.from_edge(side_seam, position_t=0.55,
                          width=36*MM, depth=65*MM)

dart_a, dart_b = original.split(ratio=0.5)

result_a = part.add_dart(dart_a, outer=True, notches=True, precision_tip=True)
result_b = part.add_dart(dart_b, outer=True, notches=True, precision_tip=True)
```

Both sub-darts share the exact same tip point; the grey overlay shows
where the original single dart would have been.

![Example 4 – One dart split into two equal sub-darts](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

---

## Example 5 — Dart Transfer (Pivot Method)

The classic **pivot method** rotates a dart around the tip to any other
edge while keeping the intake angle identical. Here a side-seam bust dart
is transferred to the shoulder seam.

```python
original = Dart.from_edge(
    side_seam, position_t=0.38,
    width=26*MM, reference_point=pts["bust_point"], tip_shortfall=20*MM,
)

transferred = transfer_dart(
    original,
    new_edge=shoulder_seam,
    new_position_t=0.55,
)
result = part.add_dart(transferred, outer=True, notches=True, precision_tip=True)
```

The grey overlay shows the original side-seam dart. The bust point (•) is
marked as the pivot. Both darts have the same `intake_angle` by
construction.

![Example 5 – Dart transferred from side seam to shoulder seam](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Style Reference

| Constant | Usage |
|----------|-------|
| `STYLE_DART_STITCH` | Dashed stitching lines on dart legs; also used for the rhombus outline |
| `STYLE_DART_FOLD` | Long-dash–dot crease/fold line from mouth center to tip |

Both constants can be passed as `stitch_style=` / `fold_style=` overrides
to `add_dart()`.

---

## Geometry Properties

```python
dart.width          # mouth opening in mm  (leg_a ↔ leg_b distance)
dart.depth          # depth in mm          (center ↔ tip distance)
dart.intake_angle   # full angle in radians (leg_a–tip–leg_b)
dart.fold_line      # Segment: center → tip
dart.stitch_line_a  # Segment: leg_a  → tip
dart.stitch_line_b  # Segment: leg_b  → tip
```

Transformations always return a **new** `Dart` (immutable-style):

```python
dart.translate(dx, dy)            # shift all four points
dart.rotate(pivot, angle_rad)     # CCW rotation — the pivot method
dart.split(ratio=0.5)             # → (dart_a, dart_b)
```
